The inverse equity hypothesis suggests that as a health program or intervention is first introduced, it tends to benefit the wealthy or higher socioeconomic groups more than the poor or lower socioeconomic groups, but as the program becomes more widespread, the benefits tend to accrue more to the poor or lower socioeconomic groups, thereby reducing health inequities.

In the context of cancer screening in middle-income countries, the inverse equity hypothesis may indeed apply. Initially, cancer screening programs may be more accessible to those with higher incomes, better education, and greater access to healthcare, which often includes the wealthy or higher socioeconomic groups. However, as these programs expand and become more integrated into the healthcare system, they may become more accessible to lower socioeconomic groups, potentially reducing disparities in cancer screening coverage.

Studies have shown that in some middle-income countries, the initial rollout of cancer screening programs, such as cervical or breast cancer screening, has indeed benefited higher socioeconomic groups more. However, as these programs have expanded and become more widespread, they have started to reach lower socioeconomic groups, reducing inequities in screening coverage.

Therefore, the inverse equity hypothesis can be applied to cancer screening in middle-income countries, highlighting the importance of continued efforts to expand and improve access to cancer screening programs, particularly for disadvantaged populations, to reduce health inequities and improve health outcomes.
